title: How an instruction names its data
objective: By the end of this lesson you can list the ways an instruction can refer to a value, explain why a reduced architecture offers so few, and map a C expression onto the instructions it becomes.

blocks.text: An instruction must say where its operands are. The set of ways it can say that is called the addressing modes, and it is one of the clearest places to see the difference between the two philosophies from earlier in this module.
The modes a reduced architecture provides

rows: Memory at register plus a constant
An address computed from the current instruction

blocks.text: That is essentially all of them. In RISC-V there is no mode that reads an address from memory and then reads again, no mode that scales an index and adds two registers, and no mode that increments a register as a side effect. That is RISC-V's choice, not a property of every reduced instruction set: aarch64 is also a RISC design and does have a scaled-index mode — you have already seen ldr w8, [x0, w1, sxtw #2] in this course — and a pre-index mode that updates the base register. Architectures with complex instruction sets have all of those, and more.

blocks.title: Fewer modes is a decision about the decoder, not about expressiveness
blocks.text: Every addressing mode is a case the hardware must handle, and each one adds a path through the address-generation logic. Keeping the set small keeps that logic shallow, which keeps the clock fast — the same reasoning as fixed-length instructions. Anything the modes cannot express is done with an extra instruction instead, and an extra instruction is cheap when instructions are fast.
What base plus offset is for

blocks.caption: The one memory mode, doing everything memory needs
lines: lw x5, 0(x6)      /* *p           — offset zero */
lw x5, 8(x6)      /* p->field     — the field's offset in the struct */
lw x5, 16(sp)     /* a local      — its slot in the stack frame */
sw x5, 4(x6)      /* p->other = x */
/* One mode covers pointer dereference, struct fields and locals,
because all three are 'a base address plus a constant displacement'.
The offset is the 12-bit immediate from the encoding lesson. */

blocks.text: What it cannot do, and what happens instead

blocks.caption: An array index, which needs arithmetic first
lines: /* C: x = a[i];  where a is int* in x10 and i is in x11 */
slli x12, x11, 2      /* i * 4, because an int is 4 bytes */
add  x12, x10, x12    /* base + scaled index */
lw   x5,  0(x12)      /* now a plain base-plus-offset load */
/* Three instructions. On x86-64 this is one, because that architecture
has a mode that scales and adds in the address calculation itself.
The reduced version is more instructions and simpler hardware —
which is the trade this whole module is about. */

blocks.title: This is why array access in a loop is worth looking at
blocks.text: If the index advances by one each iteration, the compiler can replace the multiply-and-add with a single pointer increment, turning three instructions into one. That transformation is called strength reduction, and it is one of the reasons the assembly for a loop often looks nothing like the source. Seeing the three-instruction form in generated code usually means the compiler could not prove the pattern was regular.
PC-relative addressing, and why it matters

Branches and jumps encode an offset from the current instruction rather than an absolute address. That is what allows a block of code to be loaded anywhere in memory and still work — which is exactly the address randomisation from the operating systems course. Position-independent code depends on this mode existing.

blocks.caption: Absolute versus relative, and why relative wins
lines: beq x5, x6, +16      /* jump 16 bytes forward from here */
/* If this code is loaded at a different address tomorrow, the offset
is still correct. An absolute target would have to be patched at
load time, which is what a relocation is — and why position-
independent code needs fewer of them. */

rows: x + y where both are locals in registers
The offset is known at compile time

blocks.text: The row worth noticing is the last: a constant index costs nothing extra, because the multiplication happened at compile time. A variable index costs the scaling. That difference is invisible in the source and obvious in the instructions.

blocks.title: Find each mode in generated code
steps: Write a C function using each row of the table above
Compile with: cc -S -O1 f.c -o -    and find the instruction for each
Identify which mode each instruction uses, from its operand syntax
Compare a[3] with a[i] and count the instructions each needs
Write a loop over an array and look for the strength reduction described above
Compile the same loop with -O0 and compare — the transformation should be absent
Find a branch in the output and confirm its target is expressed as an offset, not an address
Try x + 100000 and observe how the compiler builds a constant too large for one field
blocks.expected: Each addressing mode identified in real generated code, a measured difference between a constant and a variable index, and a loop whose optimised form no longer contains the multiply. The last item is the one that connects this lesson to performance: the instruction count for the same source line is a compiler decision, and you can now read which one it made.

cheatsheet: Reduced architectures offer four modes: register, immediate, base plus offset, PC-relative
One memory mode covers pointer dereference, struct fields and stack locals
The offset is the 12-bit immediate from the encoding lesson
No scaled-index mode: a[i] needs a shift and an add first
x86-64 does that in one instruction — more expressive, more decoder work
A constant index costs nothing extra; a variable index costs the scaling
Compilers replace the multiply in a loop with a pointer increment (strength reduction)
Branches use PC-relative offsets, which is what makes code position-independent
Position independence is what allows the address randomisation from the OS course

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a[i] take three instructions on a reduced architecture and one on x86-64?

choices.A: The reduced version is a compiler bug
choices.D: x86-64 has an addressing mode that scales an index and adds it during address generation

checkpoint.explanation: The reduced set does the arithmetic in separate instructions. More expressive modes mean more cases in the address-generation hardware. The reduced design pays extra instructions to keep that logic shallow, which is the trade this module keeps returning to.

checkpoint.prompt: Why do branches encode an offset rather than an absolute address?

choices.D: So the code works wherever it is loaded

checkpoint.explanation: Is what makes position-independent code and address randomisation possible. An absolute target would need patching at load time. PC-relative addressing removes that need, and it is what the operating systems course's address randomisation depends on.

checkpoint.prompt: a[3] compiles to a single load while a[i] does not. Why?

choices.A: Small indices are special-cased in hardware
choices.B: The compiler computed 3 times the element size at compile time

checkpoint.explanation: It becomes an ordinary base-plus-offset load. The scaling still happens; it just happens during compilation. A variable index cannot be resolved then, so the multiply has to appear in the instruction stream.

checkpoint.prompt: An optimised loop over an array contains no multiply, but the -O0 version does. What happened?

choices.A: The array was moved to registers
choices.D: The optimiser removed a bounds check

checkpoint.explanation: The index arithmetic was replaced by advancing a pointer once per iteration. When the index advances regularly, the address can be advanced instead of recomputed. Seeing the multiply survive usually means the compiler could not prove the access pattern was regular.
